t: Command-line reference
x: Selecting a file displays metadata. Preview or a double-click reads it. Directories expand on click and reveal more entries while scrolling. Refresh reloads the selected directory level. Raw previews request at most --preview-bytes + 1 bytes to detect truncation. Complete .json previews are formatted. CSV, JSON/JSONL, Arrow IPC, Parquet, and database relations can render as tables. Arrow IPC and Parquet use row and decoded Arrow-memory bounds. The byte option is not a universal cap on backend traffic or on all structured decoders’ allocations. SQL Preview is available when the filesystem provides query(). It accepts SELECT and WITH and wraps the query with a row limit. Downloads are copied to --download-root. Target paths remove protocol parts and unsafe . or .. components. Metadata fields depend on the backend.

t: Why browsing and previewing are separate operations
x: Why browsing and previewing are separate operations fsspec-browser treats filesystem navigation, data retrieval, and rendering as separate concerns. This makes one browser usable across local files, object stores, database relations, and any other installed fsspec backend. fsspec is the compatibility boundary The browser asks a backend for familiar operations such as ls, info, open, and get_file. It does not need a frontend-specific implementation for every storage system. Plain local paths and S3 can use native Rust backends in the terminal application; other installed protocols cross the fsspec-rs Python bridge. The web server resolves all URLs through Python fsspec. This boundary gives the browser broad backend coverage, while backend packages retain ownership of authentication, path rules, metadata, and query behavior. Selection does not imply an unbounded read Listings and metadata are normally cheap compared with downloading an object or materializing a database relation. For that reason, selecting an entry first displays its metadata. Remote file previews require an explicit action, and preview paths use byte or row limits appropriate to their format. t: Why browsing and previewing are separate operations
s: Selection does not imply an unbounded read
x: Listings and metadata are normally cheap compared with downloading an object or materializing a database relation. For that reason, selecting an entry first displays its metadata. Remote file previews require an explicit action, and preview paths use byte or row limits appropriate to their format. Database relations remain directory-like so users can browse columns, indexes, and constraints. The browser recognizes relation metadata and requests a bounded data view when previewing, rather than treating the directory as a conventional file.

t: Why browsing and previewing are separate operations
x: Backends return bytes, metadata, or Arrow tables; they do not decide how those values look on screen. The terminal renderer optimizes for a fixed cell grid and keyboard navigation. The web renderer can use scrollable tables and request another page near the end of the current one. CSV, JSON, JSONL, and Parquet need format-aware renderers to be useful, but decoding them does not change filesystem semantics. Keeping rendering in the browser prevents display concerns from leaking into storage backends.

t: Why browsing and previewing are separate operations
x: Directory paging limits how much metadata the UI presents at once. Preview paging limits rows, while the byte limit bounds generic file reads. These controls serve responsiveness and resource use. A row page does not necessarily bound backend reads, and the byte option does not cap every decoder or backend cache. Database backends can make paging efficient by pushing limit and offset into a query. Generic files may still require sequential decoding to reach a later page. The same UI gesture therefore has backend-dependent cost even though its result looks consistent.

t: How to build from source
x: How to build from source From a source checkout, install Rust, Node.js 22, and pnpm 10.28.2. Install the pinned Cargo license collector before building: cargo install cargo-bundle-licenses --version 4.2.0 --locked make develop make build Keep both Hatch hooks enabled for distribution builds. SKIP_HATCH_JS also skips pnpm license collection. Linux wheel containers install Node and pnpm to run that hook. If license collection fails, check the missing dependency against the Cargo override reference. Review dependency inventories when changing JavaScript build inputs. See License bundle reference for included files and coverage.

t: License bundle reference
x: License bundle reference Wheels include the pnpm production dependency inventory and Cargo dependency license texts under fsspec_browser/licenses. Both bundles preserve original texts and notices. The pnpm inventory excludes development tools. Cargo collection includes nonhost dependencies and is not a linked-code-only inventory. Python dependencies and separately vendored assets are outside this collection’s scope. Missing license texts fail the build. The Cargo override reference records provisional source-backed texts that require human review before shipping. Collection does not certify license compliance. SKIP_HATCH_JS skips JavaScript building and pnpm license collection. Distribution builds require both hooks; Linux wheel containers install Node and pnpm.

t: Cargo license overrides
x: Cargo license overrides license-overrides.json supplies texts that cargo-bundle-licenses 4.2.0 does not discover for the locked dependencies. Entries match exact package name, version, and license identifier. license-provenance.json records original source locations and SHA-256 hashes. These overrides are provisional and require human review before shipping. They do not change the declared license choices or certify compatibility, notice sufficiency, or source-availability requirements.
